stem: Vikram builds two shapes from the same $9$ unit squares, side-aligned with no gaps. Shape $P$ is a $3$-by-$3$ square. Shape $Q$ is an L-shape made by moving squares.

parts.text: Which claim correctly compares area and perimeter?

options.text: Area and perimeter both stay the same for every rearrangement of the $9$ squares.
Changing the arrangement creates the $9$ unit squares.
Area stays the same because both shapes use $9$ unit squares, but the perimeter can change.
Only Shape $P$ has an area, because it is a square.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

part_answers.answer: Same number of unit squares means equal area; different outlines can share different numbers of edges, so perimeters need not match.

teacher.key_rationale: Equal count of unit squares keeps area $9$, while rearranging can change how many outer edges remain, so perimeter can differ. Treating both as fixed, reversing arrangement and squares, or denying area for the L-shape miss that hinge.
